https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Nazir Afzal, who was head of the CPS in the north-west of England from 2011 to 2015, is now chancellor of the University of Manchester. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Nazir Afzal, who was head of the CPS in the north-west of England from 2011 to 2015, is now chancellor of the University of Manchester. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Jason Arday Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday review Nazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his death Richard Adams Education editor Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.48 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The University of Cambridge has asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, to lead the first part of its review into the death of the scholar Jason Arday. Arday died at his home in south London on 14 August, nine days after his resignation as a Cambridge professor amid swirling allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career. Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said the time since Arday’s death had been “a period of profound sadness and reflection” for the university, and she sought to defend her institution from criticism. “We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus but given the devastating outcome, we are all asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more. This review will answer that question,” Prentice said. “We are committed to ensuring that any recommendations arising from the review are addressed and adopted with clear accountability for delivering necessary changes.” View image in fullscreen Jason Arday was found dead at home in south London on 14 August. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian Arday was named professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, with the university highlighting his appointment as the university’s youngest ever black professor at the age of 37. Arday denied accusations of plagiarism levelled against him but on 5 August the university said it would hold an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours after the investigation was announced. Prentice said the review would be in two parts, with the first, led by Afzal, to focus on the support given to Arday in the immediate period before his death. Afzal said: “I am honoured to have been asked to lead part one of this important independent review. At its heart is a person, a family and a community who have been profoundly affected by Professor Arday’s death. It is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity. “My responsibility will be to listen carefully, examine the evidence thoroughly and understand what support, interventions and protections were available to Professor Arday in the period before his death. We must be willing to ask difficult questions, including whether more could and should have been done. This work will be conducted independently and with urgency.” Afzal, a University of Birmingham graduate, is the chancellor of the University of Manchester, having been head of the CPS in the north-west of England during which he prosecuted child exploitation rings in Rochdale. In 2022 he led an independent review into London fire brigade that exposed a culture of misogyny, racism and bullying. Prentice said: “I am very grateful to Nazir for agreeing to lead this part of the review. He is a highly respected legal professional who will ask challenging questions about the support that was offered to Professor Arday during his time at Cambridge.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Jason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue research Read more The university said the review’s second stage would consider “the wider context of Professor Arday’s time at the university”, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, the university’s response to allegations of research misconduct, and the support it gave to academics “subject to extraordinary public and media scrutiny”. Cambridge said it would appoint an independent external chair for the second part and an expert panel “including individuals with lived experience” to advise the review. It said part one of the review was expected to report within three months, and the second part within six months of establishing the expert panel. Earlier this week, Jacqui Smith, the minister responsible for higher education, told parliament that she was “more than just keeping an eye” on Cambridge’s response to Arday’s death. Smith said England’s higher education regulator, the Office for Students, had the powers to investigate further if necessary. Text Groups eNewsletter Facebook Twitter Instagram Pinterest Youtube Soundcloud Faith Request Prayer Thought For The Day Our Catholic Faith Rosary Traditional Prayers Confession Find a Mass Daily Readings Catholic News Diocese of Saint Petersburg Listen Live Spirit FM 90.5 (HD1) The Light (HD2) El Fuego (HD3) Give Now Catholic News How one Lithuanian cardinal resisted Soviet persecution from a KGB prison cell http://www.myspiritfm.com/News?blogid=Catholic-News&view=post&articleid=302846&link=1&fldKeywords=&fldAuthor=&fldTopic=0 A new biography traces Cardinal Sigitas Tamkevicius' imprisonment by the KGB and his decades leading Lithuania's underground Catholic resistance to Soviet persecution. A new biography published in Lithuania recounts the life of Cardinal Sigitas Tamkevicius, SJ, one of the leading Catholic figures in the resistance to Soviet religious persecution. It details his work as editor of the underground Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Lithuania publication and his subsequent imprisonment by the KGB. Written by journalist Regina Statkuviene and published by the DONUM Foundation , "In the Light of the Altar" draws on recent interviews she conducted with Tamkevicius. The book also includes his letters and diary entries alongside accounts of his childhood, priesthood, underground activities, imprisonment, exile, and later episcopal ministry. Tamkevicius was arrested in 1983 and sentenced to six years in a strict-regime labor camp followed by four years of exile in Siberia. His story offers an insight into the experience of Catholics who resisted the Soviet Union's efforts to suppress religious life and impose state atheism. Sigitas Tamkevicius stands for a portrait during his military service in the Soviet Army in Khosta, Russia, in 1959. | Credit: Photo courtesy of Cardinal Sigitas Tamkevicius Catholic resistance in Soviet-occupied Lithuania Founded by Tamkevicius in 1972, the Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Lithuania ("Lietuvos kataliku bažnycios kronika," or "LKB Kronika") was an underground publication documenting religious persecution and human rights abuses in Soviet-occupied Lithuania. The Kronika recorded arrests and interrogations of clergy and lay Catholics, confiscation of Church property, restrictions on religious practice, and attempts by Soviet authorities to infiltrate the Church. It was a strictly factual catalog of human rights violations, not a literary magazine or a platform for theological commentary. Its reports were secretly typed and reproduced, with editions being smuggled to Western diplomats and foreign journalists in Moscow, with activists often microfilming the pages and hiding the negatives inside everyday objects like book covers or flashlights. Once in the West, the material was translated and disseminated internationally, including through Vatican Radio and Radio Free Europe, directly challenging Soviet claims that religious freedom existed behind the Iron Curtain. Sigitas Tamkevicius, first from left, stands with fellow seminarians at his ordination to the priesthood in May 1962. | Credit: Photo courtesy of Cardinal Sigitas Tamkevicius In the book's foreword, Archbishop Petar Rajic, current prefect of the Papal Household and former apostolic nuncio to Lithuania, described Tamkevicius as one of the most prominent witnesses to the Soviet era. "Every Catholic who loves the Church should read the Chronicle," Rajic wrote, calling it a testimony to the spiritual strength and resistance of the Lithuanian people, rooted in the victory of the cross of Christ and offering lessons for Catholics today and future generations. Arrest and KGB interrogation The Kronika not only exposed Soviet religious persecution to the outside world but also strengthened the underground Catholic resistance within Lithuania. The KGB consequently intensified efforts to identify and suppress those involved in producing and distributing the publication. Cardinal Sigitas Tamkevicius reaches into the hiding place in the altar of the church in Simnas, Lithuania, where he once concealed copies of the underground Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Lithuania, in 2021. | Credit: Jurate Tamošiunyte-Karašauskiene Since Tamkevicius openly preached against state atheism and challenged Soviet restrictions on the Church, he was seen as a visible figure within the Catholic resistance movement. The Soviet authorities eventually arrested Tamkevicius in May 1983 and charged him with "anti-Soviet agitation and propaganda." After six months of pretrial detention in the KGB isolation prison in Vilnius, he was sentenced in December to six years in a strict-regime labor camp in the Ural Mountains, followed by four years of exile in Siberia. During his detention, Tamkevicius recalled psychological pressure from KGB interrogators. On one occasion, an interrogator offered him tea and biscuits. He drank the tea at around 2 p.m. and soon became extremely dizzy. His next clear memory came hours later, when he heard the interrogator angrily questioning him about a document concerning the underground seminary. He was then told that it was already 10 p.m. "Only then did I realize that after drinking the tea I had lost consciousness," he recalled. Tamkevicius believed he had been drugged to extract information from him. The attempt failed. "Seeing how angry the interrogator was, I understood that he had managed to extract nothing from me," he said. Life in the labor camp Tamkevicius recalled that his first assignment in the labor camp was peeling potatoes. "Each potato had to be taken out of almost ice-cold water," he recalled. He feared that doing this for six years would make him ill, but after two weeks he was transferred to a metalworking workshop, where he collected metal shavings from lathes and carried them to containers. Prisoners worked eight hours a day and were allotted another eight hours for sleep. The food was poor, consisting largely of "thin soup and watery porridge." Later, after Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in 1985, Tamkevicius was assigned to the camp kitchen and had to rise at 4 a.m. to prepare breakfast. The ingredients were often badly preserved. Fish, he recalled, could be heavily salted and stored for years. He learned to make the most of what was available, washing the fish overnight and frying it separately so that prisoners could have a more edible meal. During more than five years in captivity, Tamkevicius was transferred under guard seven times and encountered prisoners ranging from teenagers to murderers. The experience became for him a reflection on human nature and the consequences of abandoning moral law. "A life without God, without the commandments of the Decalogue, a life without love," he wrote, describing the selfishness, pride, lust, and greed that shaped much of prison life. His reflections ultimately turned toward his own imprisonment and vocation. "Lord, what was it that brought me behind bars and barbed wire?" he asked. "The affairs of the Church? Yes. Concern for people's moral lives? Yes. Living according to my conscience? Yes. Thank you, Lord, that the answer was 'yes.'" For Tamkevicius, imprisonment was ultimately the consequence of refusing to compromise his faith in the face of communist oppression. Bishop Sigitas Tamkevicius addresses young people gathered to meet Pope John Paul II at the Darius and Girenas Stadium in Kaunas, Lithuania, in September 1993. | Credit: Photo courtesy of Cardinal Sigitas Tamkevicius From persecution to freedom Tamkevicius was released in 1988 as Soviet repression began to weaken. He returned to Lithuania as the country moved toward independence, restored on March 11, 1990. Tamkevicius' story offers a firsthand account of the cost of defending the faith under communism and the role of ordinary believers in preserving the Church through decades of persecution. https://wiky.com/2026/09/02/climate-shoc.text: Sign In Search NEWS ON AIR EVENTS BLOGS PODCASTS WEATHER Climate shocks hit EU maize heartland in Hungary and Romania By Thomson Reuters Sep 2, 2026 | 5:15 AM By Krisztina Fenyo, Luiza Ilie, Gergely Szakacs and Gus Trompiz HAJDUSZOBOSZLO, Hungary, Sept 2 (Reuters) – Standing in a field of withered maize in northeast Hungary, farmer Karoly Kovacs recalls harvests that now seem almost unimaginable. “I could hardly believe when we reaped 17 tons a hectare back around 2010,” Kovacs said. “But then, we used to have 1,000 millimetres of rain and now, almost nothing.” For farmers across central and eastern Europe, what was ​once an occasional drought has become a recurring threat. Record heatwaves and chronic water shortages are shrinking maize harvests, forcing some growers to abandon ‌the crop and reshaping a region long seen as a pillar of European grain production. The impact is most evident in Hungary and Romania, two key European Union maize producers where acreage has fallen sharply in recent years. Hungary, once a regular exporter, is set to import maize this year, while Romania’s exportable surplus has dwindled. The EU’s maize harvest, typically its second-largest cereals crop, is forecast at 50.1 million metric tons this year, according to the European Commission’s late-August estimate. That would be a near two-decade low and about a fifth below the average of the past three ‌years. “If we ​see this continuity of dry summers for the next campaigns, this is a very big story for the ⁠EU if the corn acreage and/or corn yields ⁠keep decreasing,” said Gabriel Antonio, a commodity market analyst at Expana, who projects an 8% to 9% increase in EU maize imports in 2026/2027. While Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, central Europe faces particularly acute pressures from heat, soil moisture deficits and water shortages, Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data show. Romania and Hungary, where maize acreage has plummeted in recent years, perform worse than both the EU and OECD averages for soil moisture anomalies. “This sustained decline ​in soil moisture has direct implications for agricultural productivity and water resource management and, therefore, food security and livelihoods,” the OECD said in an emailed response to questions. Over the past decade, Hungary’s June and July highs have exceeded the 1961 to 1990 average by 3.1 degrees Celsius (5.6 degrees Fahrenheit), according to Reuters Climate Monitor ⁠data. Romania is close behind, with average summer highs 3 C (5.4 F) above historical norms. Romania’s maize ⁠crop is expected to total around 8 million tons this year, having escaped the worst of this year’s European drought but ​still down more than half from 2018 to 2019 levels. Hungary’s estimated 2.5-million-ton harvest would be less than a third of its output during those years. Romania’s maize exports ​fell to between 2.2 million and 4.7 million tons between 2023 and 2025 from more than 7 million tons around the turn ‌of the decade, European Commission figures show. Hungary, usually an exporter, will have to import maize this year, the government said. ‘SEMI-DESERT CLIMATE’ Tamas Petohazi, chairman of the Association of Hungarian Grain Growers, said many farmers have given up the business altogether, while others have taken second jobs because family farms can no longer support them. “We need a paradigm shift,” Petohazi said, adding the lack of rain, which forced shutdowns at nuclear reactors in Hungary and Romania last month as the Danube River receded, meant Hungary was ⁠heading for what he called a semi-desert climate. The European Commission’s 10-year outlook for agricultural markets, published in December, put yield uncertainty for maize in eastern Europe at 18.7% in 2035, the highest among the global regions it monitors. Kovacs said that if current climate trends persist, he may eventually abandon maize cultivation. He is considering diversifying into ⁠dry pasta production using eggs from his chickens. ‘PLANT MAIZE AND ‌HARVEST NOTHING’ Cezar Gheorghe of consultancy AGRIColumn said climate change has been a major factor behind falling maize acreage in ⁠Romania, encouraging a shift to autumn crops and hitting small farmers especially hard. “From 2020 until today, they plant maize ​and harvest nothing. ‌Why would you keep doing it?,” he said. “The same with medium-sized farms — they sowed, everything went well during the ​vegetation period, and ⁠then the drought began, which effectively scorched large swathes of the country.” Romanian farmer Stefan Moraru has shifted to sunflowers because they require less water than maize. “A watershed year for us was 2020. Across all our crops we suffered losses,” he said, adding the poor harvest triggered his move to invest into irrigation. But even that strategy has its limits. A canal supplying water to his farms has been idle since mid-July. “The problem is that nature is not co-operating,” he said. “You can buy pivots, pumps, pipelines and irrigation equipment, but without water they become useless. Water is the key factor. Without it, all these investments amount to zero.” (Graphics and data analysis by Ben Welsh and Jack WalkerAdditional reporting ​by Ovidiu Micsik. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly.text: Image source, Reuters By Grace Eliza Goodwin Published 10 October 2026, 16:28 BST Updated 19 minutes ago US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said. The 50-year-old murderer has been returned to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison. Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition. Earlier this week, she regained consciousness and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," her lawyers said in their statement. Pike's case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection. At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he does not know whether the state intends to try to execute her again. The judge also ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state. Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people. Image source, Family handout Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and Shipp After Pike survived the two lethal injections, she lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital. For days, her legal team believed she was brain dead, and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment. She eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyer Randy Spivey said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?" At a press conference on Wednesday, Pike's lawyers said she was shackled to the bed and suffering from pneumonia, significant swelling on her arms, and was unable to swallow. "We don't know the toll all of this will take" on her mental health, Spivey said at the time, noting she felt "angry and confused". It's not clear what medical care Pike is receiving back in prison, but her lawyers previously said she faced a "long road to recovery". https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: The fire at mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest, on 24 October. Photograph: Berchtesgaden/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The fire at mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest, on 24 October. Photograph: Berchtesgaden/AFP/Getty Images Adolf Hitler Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest retreat was torched in an arson attack. Should it be rebuilt? With the far right resurgent in Germany, experts are divided as to whether the dictator’s former mountaintop retreat is better restored or left a ruin Deborah Cole in Berlin Sun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O ne of the last structural relics of Adolf Hitler’s dictatorship was conceived to project indomitable power. Last month it was destroyed in a suspected arson attack. Will it, and should it, be rebuilt? The historic Nazi mountaintop retreat known as the Eagle’s Nest is perched on an Alpine peak at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft), with stunning views over southern Germany and Austria. In German, its design is known as Überwältigungsarchitektur , intended to overwhelm and intimidate. Now, despite the efforts of 200 firefighters battling through the night , only charred ruins remain of the former guest lodge, tourist magnet and remembrance site destroyed in the blaze which started on 23 October. It is closed indefinitely. “Even if a British air force bomb had struck the building on 25 April 1945, as it did most of the other structures in what was then the ‘Führer’s no-go zone’ on the Obersalzberg near Berchtesgaden, Hitler’s former tea house … could scarcely have been more severely damaged than it was by the fire,” Munich’s Süddeutsche newspaper said. View image in fullscreen A brass-plated lift, built into the rock, took 41 seconds to bring visitors up to the Eagle’s Nest. Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/Alamy The fire has triggered a debate about whether, and how, to rebuild at the toxic site for the next generation of visitors, while mitigating the never-quite-banished risk of creating a shrine for neo-Nazis. While the places associated with Hitler’s victims, including the former concentration camps, are preserved in perpetuity, the question of how to treat the perpetrators’ artefacts remains fraught, particularly given the resurgence of the far right in Germany and in Europe more broadly. Local authorities believe the fire was deliberately started by a 33-year-old suspect with a history of mental illness. The site, which is owned by the German state of Bavaria, attracts more than 300,000 people each year but was closed to visitors that day. No one was injured. View image in fullscreen The Eagle’s Nest is known more prosaically in German as the Kehlsteinhaus , for the mountain it rests on. Photograph: DEA/W. BUSS/De Agostini/Getty Images Bavarian state culture minister Markus Blume has said a commission of experts in heritage conservation, construction and Germany’s culture of Holocaust remembrance would be enlisted to help determine the future of the Eagle’s Nest. Given the building’s inextricable links to the Nazi regime and its crimes, Blume said, “any reconstruction must do justice to this historical responsibility”. The marvel of Alpine engineering, which took 3,800 workers just over a year to build , is known more prosaically in German as the Kehlsteinhaus , for the mountain it rests on. After a coach ride on serpentine roads through five tunnels, visitors rode a brass-plated lift, built into the rock, for 41 seconds to reach its portal. View image in fullscreen The Eagle’s Nest pictured in 2019. Photograph: Maurice Savage/Alamy “The prestige project and the road leading to it cost about 30 million Reichsmarks, equivalent to about 130 million British pounds today,” said Nazi-era historian Felix Bohr, author of Before the Downfall: Hitler’s Years in the Wolf’s Lair, which is being published in the UK in November. “Hitler loved architecture that made other people look small. He insisted on being involved in the planning and construction of propaganda buildings.” The lodge was completed in 1938, and mainly used to welcome and impress state guests, diplomats and select foreign journalists. Just a short distance down the mountain at the Obersalzberg complex was Hitler’s own residence, the Berghof, where he spent about a quarter of his 12 years in office. View image in fullscreen The Eagle’s Nest pictured in 1940. Photograph: Hulton Deutsch/Corbis/Getty Images “Important decisions about prosecution and crime, about war and genocide were taken there,” said Sven Keller, director of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, an educational facility at the site. “The surrounding mountain scenery was used as a backdrop for the construction of Hitler’s ‘Führer’ image. It offered spectacular, awe-inspiring views, and demonstrated technical prowess to subjugate even this rough natural environment.” Inside, it had many of the trappings of Nazi bling, including Untersberg marble donated by Mussolini, Venetian mirrors and plump green leather armchairs recalling an English country manor house. Hitler is known to have visited the Eagle’s Nest only 14 times until 1939 and then never again due to the second world war’s outbreak, when the tea house no longer matched the warrior-statesman image he wished to project, Bohr said. Close associates including his companion Eva Braun still used it regularly, however. View image in fullscreen Heinrich Hoffmann, Eva Braun and Adolf Hitler at the Berghof in 1942. Photograph: Prisma by Dukas Presseagentur GmbH/Alamy After the war, Obersalzberg became a recreation centre for occupying US troops, but the last vestiges of the Berghof were torn down and hundreds of trees were planted in its place – a fateful decision that has served as a cautionary tale. “The Americans and the Bavarian state tried to prevent it from becoming a pilgrimage site for old Nazis and Hitler admirers. It didn’t work. If anything, a hidden site in the woods is even more interesting and mysterious,” Keller said. Nazi swastikas were often found carved into the tree bark. He said a 180-degree pivot toward clearly marking the site and exposing its history, including how it fit into the Nazi power apparatus, proved the healthier approach. “Public accessibility creates transparency whereas barriers or fences encourage rumours and legends,” Keller said. “Today, a popular public trail crosses the site, and mundane activities such as hiking keep it from becoming a sacred space (for neo-Nazis).” View image in fullscreen Hitler with Eva Braun at the Berghof in June 1942. Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/Alamy Keller said transparency should be the watchword going forward. “I cannot imagine that those responsible would opt for [a] simple reproduction of Nazi architecture, but it also can’t be left as a ruin – those tend to be even more fascinating,” he said. “Instead, we should find ways to integrate the material remains and new information and education, showing the temporal layers, including the use as a tourist destination since the 1950s. The fire added a new layer to the history to Obersalzberg, and this should be visible too.” New political realities in Germany and Austria, where the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) and Freedom Party lead the respective national polls, will have to be taken into account as well, he said. View image in fullscreen A US soldier at the Eagle’s Nest, 4 May 1945. Photograph: Eric Schwab/AFP/Getty Images Bohr said that troubling context led him to oppose any reconstruction of the Eagle’s Nest. “Hitler’s megalomania should remain a ruin. My suggestion would be to secure the remaining structure as far as possible and to use it to convey the history of the site,” he said. “Particularly in view of the strength of the AfD and the rise of right-wing extremism in Germany, the focus should be on coming to terms with Nazi ideology, not on restoring its stage sets.” Explore more on these topics Adolf Hitler Nazism Germany Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
